title: How I’d actually build a conversational data layer
body_markdown:
This article is contributed by:[Sandeep Singh](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sandeep-singh-7340b26/)


Architecture, semantics, and guardrails — Part 2 of 2


In Part 1, I argued that the modern BI stack is broken because there’s no real translation layer between business questions and data systems. Today, that translation is a human — and humans don’t scale.


This post is about what I think replaces them.


The short version: a **conversational intelligence layer** that handles the translation automatically, grounds the AI in your actual business semantics, and is wrapped in guardrails strong enough for enterprise use. Let me walk through it.


### The pipeline


The core flow is five stages, end to end:


1. A user submits a business question in plain English
2. A semantic mapping stage parses it against your business definitions
3. The system generates optimized SQL for your specific database
4. The query runs live against the source — no extracts, no caches
5. The result comes back as a summary, chart, or recommended action


Press enter or click to view image in full size


What makes this work in production isn’t the pipeline itself — it’s everything wrapped around it.


### The four capabilities users actually feel


From the outside, this layer does four things that traditional BI cannot.


**Ask in plain English.** No SQL, no filter menus. A regional manager types “show me retention trends for enterprise accounts in Q1” and gets a verified answer.


**Direct live access.** The engine connects to source systems — Snowflake, PostgreSQL, Iceberg, S3 — instead of stale extracts. Every answer reflects current state.


**Self-service at scale.** When the technical barrier disappears, expect roughly a 2x increase in self-serve data access within a quarter of deployment. Analysts stop being a help desk.


**Proactive insights.** The system surfaces anomalies and trends without being prompted. It understands business context well enough to volunteer what matters.


### Semantic intelligence — the part that prevents disasters


The single biggest fear about putting AI between users and data is hallucination. What happens when the model invents a column? Joins the wrong tables? Confidently returns nonsense?


This is solved with a multi-layered semantic architecture that anchors AI in business reality.


**Context-enriched AI** uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation to feed the model metadata about your tables and relationships.


**Metadata anchoring** trains it on data dictionaries — so “Revenue” in finance means something different than “Sales” in marketing, and it knows the difference.


**Refined accuracy** comes from merging LLM reasoning with a deterministic semantic layer, mitigating wrong joins and misleading interpretations.


**A business KPI layer** centralizes metric definitions, so every user gets the same answer regardless of how they phrased the question.


This is the difference between a clever AI demo and a system you’d actually trust with your numbers.


### Guardrails — because trust isn’t optional


In an enterprise context, an AI that *might* leak data or *might* run a runaway query isn’t deployable. Period.


Four guardrails do the work.


**Query validation** scans every AI-generated SQL statement for malicious patterns or inefficient joins *before* execution.


**Scoped responses** enforce role-based access control — users only see data they’re authorized to view.


**Audit logging** keeps a full trail of natural-language questions and translated SQL, for compliance and fine-tuning.


**Safe outputs** prevent hallucinated entities and keep responses inside the bounds of your data dictionary.


Like an iceberg, most of this work happens beneath the surface. The user just sees an answer. Security, compliance, and finance see a system they can sign off on.


### The architecture


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Five components, each replaceable, each observable.


**Conversational UI** handles input and renders insights.


**Semantic engine** maps natural language to metadata and manages the RAG pipeline.


**NL-to-SQL driver** generates and optimizes queries for your specific dialect.


**Guardrail proxy** validates everything for security, RBAC, and cost limits.


**Multi-source integration** connects directly to wherever your data lives.


This isn’t a monolith. Each layer can be swapped, scaled, or replaced as the underlying tech evolves — which it will.


### What actually changes


The headline number — 2x self-serve access in a quarter — matters, but it’s not the most interesting outcome.


The interesting shift is cultural. When anyone in the organization can ask the data a question and get a trustworthy answer in seconds, the relationship between business and analytics changes. Analysts stop firefighting and start building. Managers stop guessing and start testing. Decisions get made closer to the data, and faster.


The dashboard era gave us visibility. The conversational era gives us *agency* .


### Closing thought


If you’re thinking about building or buying something in this space, the questions worth asking aren’t about model accuracy on benchmarks. They’re about semantic grounding, guardrails, and how the system behaves on the messy edges of your real data.


That’s where most of these projects either succeed or quietly fail.


Your dashboards aren’t going away. But they’re about to stop being the main way you talk to your data.


*If you missed Part 1 — the case for why the modern BI stack is quietly broken — it’s worth reading first. This piece builds on it.*
